warmup.q: You read the first eight bytes of java/lang/Object.class from the JDK you're running. They are ca fe ba be 00 00 00 45. Which JDK is it?
options: You can't tell from the bytes
warmup.why: After the magic number CAFEBABE come the minor version (00 00) and the major version (00 45, which is 69). From Java 5 on, the Java version is major minus 44, so 69 is Java 25. JDK 21's own classes say 00 41 (65), and Java 8's say 00 34 (52). The first section reads these bytes with a small program.

opening:
A theatre's prompt book follows a strict layout. The first page carries a stamp naming the edition of the house rules it follows. Then comes the glossary, a numbered list of every name the book uses, and then the cues. A company that wanted to print its own pages had to borrow a printing press from outside, and get a new one each time the house rules changed.

A class file is that kind of page, and its house rules change with every JDK release, every six months. In the last lesson, Byte Buddy wrote subclasses and handed their bytes to a class loader. It prints them with a press it carries inside, a copy of a library called ASM. Since JDK 24, Java has a press of its own: the ClassFile API.

The easy trap is trusting a page because it printed. A class can build, pass the JVM's checks and load, and still compute the wrong answer. In this lesson, we'll read a class file's first bytes by hand, read the same class with the ClassFile API, print a new class from scratch, and edit one safely. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a prompt book's strict layout: a stamp, a glossary, then the cues. We read that layout byte by byte. Then the JDK's own press read it as models and elements, printed a new Fade, proofread it with verify, and copied it into FadeV2 line by line.

Now look for a test in your project that only checks that generated code loads, or that a class verifies. Add one assertion on what the code computes.

Next, we'll stop making new classes and change one that is already running. How does an agent slip a note into a class before it loads, or even after?

sections.h: Reading the page by hand: magic number, version and the glossary
sections.html:
Every tool in this track reads or writes the same format: javap, the verifier (the JVM's check that bytecode is type-safe), Proxy, the lambda machinery, Byte Buddy, and the agents of the next lesson. A class file is an array of bytes with a fixed layout, set out in chapter 4 of the JVM specification. Here are the first ten bytes of java/lang/Object.class on JDK 25, as this section's demo prints them:

ca fe ba be  00 00  00 45  00 73
magic        minor  major  constant_pool_count

The first four bytes are the magic number, 0xCAFEBABE: the stamp that says "this is a class file". Then come two version numbers. The major version is 0x45, which is 69, and Java 25 wrote it. From Java 5 on, the Java version is the major version minus 44. A JVM refuses a class file whose major version is newer than its own, with UnsupportedClassVersionError. The labs' own classes say 00 41, which is 65, because the build compiles them with release 21.

Then comes constant_pool_count, and after it the constant pool itself: lesson 2's glossary, a numbered table of every name and constant the class uses. Every number in the file is big-endian, biggest byte first, which is exactly how DataInputStream reads. So the first four fields take four lines:

Java
DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes));
int magic = in.readInt();               // u4: 0xCAFEBABE
int minor = in.readUnsignedShort();     // u2
int major = in.readUnsignedShort();     // u2: 65 = Java 21, 69 = Java 25
int poolCount = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1
Kotlin
val input = DataInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(bytes))
val magic = input.readInt()                // u4: 0xCAFEBABE
val minor = input.readUnsignedShort()      // u2
val major = input.readUnsignedShort()      // u2: 65 = Java 21, 69 = Java 25
val poolCount = input.readUnsignedShort()  // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1

The glossary is the hard part. Each entry starts with a one-byte tag, and the tag decides how many bytes follow. A Utf8 entry, a piece of text, has a two-byte length and then the text. A Class entry has two bytes: the number of the Utf8 entry that holds the class's name. A Methodref, a reference to a method, has four. And a Long or Double entry takes up two numbers. Remember lesson 2's javap -v listing of StackDemo:

   #7 = Long               1000l
   #9 = InvokeDynamic      #0:#10         // #0:makeConcatWithConstants:(JLjava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;

There is no #8, because the 8-byte constant at #7 sits in two seats. After the glossary come the access flags, then this_class, the number of the Class entry that names this class. Then come the superclass, the interfaces, the fields, the methods and the attributes. In the lab, you write this walk yourself and check it against a real class-file library.

Each entry's size depends on its tag, so one wrong count shifts everything after it. Count Long and Double twice.

That walk is the reason a library helps. Anything that writes or changes classes must get this format exactly right, and the format gains a new major version every six months, sometimes with new kinds of entries. Until JDK 24, the JDK had no public library for it. Frameworks bundled ASM, the long-standing class-file library (Byte Buddy carries its own copy), and needed a new release for each new class-file version. The JDK kept a private copy of ASM too; it's gone from the jdk-25-ga source.

Doing the walk by hand once teaches you the format. Doing it for every class, on every JDK, is a job for a press.

try.title: Read three class-file headers
steps: Before you run anything, predict the major version of ClassFileHeader.class (built by the labs), of java.lang.Object on the JDK you're using, and of kotlin.Unit from the Kotlin standard library.

If you have both JDK 21 and JDK 25 installed, run the Java version on each, from labs/: java -cp bytecode/build/classes/java/demo:bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.bytecode.l06.ClassFileHeader.

code.title: ClassFileHeader.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l06; import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream; import java.io.DataInputStream; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; import java.util.HexFormat; /** The first ten bytes of three class files: magic, version and constant pool size. */ public class ClassFileHeader { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { show(ClassFileHeader.class); // compiled by the labs build with release 21 show(HeaderMarker.class); // compiled by kotlinc in the same build (from ClassFileHeader.kt) show(Object.class); // from the JDK you are running } static void show(Class<?> c) throws IOException { byte[] bytes; try (InputStream in = c.getResourceAsStream(c.getSimpleName() + ".class")) { bytes = in.readAllBytes(); } DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)); int magic = in.readInt(); // u4 int minor = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2 int major = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2 int poolCount = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 System.out.printf("%-34s %s magic=%X version=%d.%d (Java %d) pool entries=%d size=%d bytes%n", c.getName(), HexFormat.ofDelimiter(" ").formatHex(bytes, 0, 10), magic, major, minor, major - 44, poolCount - 1, bytes.length); } }

alt.title: ClassFileHeader.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l06 import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream import java.io.DataInputStream import java.util.HexFormat /** A Kotlin class for the Java twin to read. */ class HeaderMarker /** The first ten bytes of three class files: magic, version and constant pool size. */ fun main() { show(HeaderMarker::class.java) // compiled by kotlinc in the labs build with jvmTarget 21 show(Unit::class.java) // the Kotlin standard library jar show(Any::class.java) // java.lang.Object, from the JDK you are running } private fun show(c: Class<*>) { val bytes = c.getResourceAsStream(c.simpleName + ".class")!!.use { it.readAllBytes() } val input = DataInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)) val magic = input.readInt() // u4 val minor = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2 val major = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2 val poolCount = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 println("%-34s %s magic=%X version=%d.%d (Java %d) pool entries=%d size=%d bytes".format( c.name, HexFormat.ofDelimiter(" ").formatHex(bytes, 0, 10), magic, major, minor, major - 44, poolCount - 1, bytes.size)) }

try.expect: Every line starts with ca fe ba be. The labs' own classes, Java and Kotlin, are version=65.0 (Java 21), because the build uses release 21 and jvmTarget 21. java.lang.Object is 65.0 (Java 21) with 123 pool entries on JDK 21, and 69.0 (Java 25) with 114 on JDK 25, so the same program reports the JDK it runs on. kotlin.Unit is 52.0 (Java 8): the standard library is compiled for Java 8, so it runs everywhere.

refs.title: JVM Specification SE 25, chapter 4: The class File Format

video.title: A class file is bytes with a fixed layout; the ClassFile API parses them into elements, builds classes from builder lambdas, and transforms them as a flatMap: each element in, zero or more out

sections.h: Reading it with the ClassFile API: models and elements
sections.html:
The package java.lang.classfile is the JDK's own class-file library. It was a preview feature in JDK 22 (JEP 457) and JDK 23 (JEP 466), and became final in JDK 24 (JEP 484). So on JDK 25 you use it with no special flags. A preview feature is a complete design that you can only use with --enable-preview, while the JDK team collects feedback. The labs compile with release 21, which can't see the package, so this lesson's ClassFile API code lives in single-file programs under labs/bytecode/preview/. You run them with java File.java on JDK 24 or later. On JDK 21 they stop at once with package java.lang.classfile does not exist.

Everything starts at ClassFile.of(). Its parse method turns bytes into a ClassModel:

Java
ClassModel cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes);
System.out.println(cm.thisClass().asInternalName() + " major " + cm.majorVersion());
for (MethodModel m : cm.methods()) {
    long invokes = m.code()
            .map(code -> code.elementStream().filter(e -> e instanceof InvokeInstruction).count())
            .orElse(0L);
    System.out.println(m.methodName().stringValue() + m.methodType().stringValue() + " invokes=" + invokes);
}
Kotlin
val cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes)
println("${cm.thisClass().asInternalName()} major ${cm.majorVersion()}")
for (m in cm.methods()) {
    val invokes = m.code()
        .map { code -> code.elementStream().filter { it is InvokeInstruction }.count() }
        .orElse(0L)
    println("${m.methodName().stringValue()}${m.methodType().stringValue()} invokes=$invokes")
}

A model is an immutable description of one part of a class file: the class, a field, a method, or a method's code. Picture the press reading a page into a stack of typed cards. The package documentation adds that a ClassModel "is inflated lazily; most parts of the classfile are not parsed until they are actually needed". So a broken method can parse fine, and throw IllegalArgumentException only when you open it.

Each model can also be read as a sequence of elements, its cards in order. A class's elements are its methods, fields and attributes. A method's code is a sequence of instructions, labels and other code elements. Each instruction is an object with a type you can test, such as InvokeInstruction, ConstantInstruction or InvokeDynamicInstruction. The rest of the API is built on this one idea. Reading walks the elements, building writes elements, and transforming maps elements to elements.

Let's point it at lesson 2's StackDemo, the class with the lighting fade. ClassFileTour parses it, counts the glossary entries by kind, and counts the invoke instructions in each method. On JDK 25 it prints:

workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo extends java/lang/Object, major 65
constant pool: {ClassEntry=7, FieldRefEntry=1, InvokeDynamicEntry=1, LongEntry=2, MethodHandleEntry=1, MethodRefEntry=5, NameAndTypeEntry=7, StringEntry=2, Utf8Entry=43}
  <init>()V  invokes=1
  seconds(JI)J  invokes=0
  describe(Ljava/lang/String;J)Ljava/lang/String;  invokes=0
  main([Ljava/lang/String;)V  invokes=3

The two LongEntry cards are the 1000 and the 32 from the fade. seconds(JI)J does arithmetic and calls nothing. describe builds a string with +, and yet its count is 0. Keep that in mind for the Try it.

Names and types come back as glossary entries. methodName() is a Utf8Entry, which is why the code calls stringValue(). When you build a class, you go the other way. You pass symbolic descriptions from java.lang.constant, such as ClassDesc.of("Fade") for a class or MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long) for a method type, and the library creates the entries.

Reading is half of what a press does. The other half is printing.

try.title: Tour lesson 2's class with the ClassFile API
steps: This needs JDK 24 or later. From labs/, make sure lesson 2's demo was built (./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.StackDemo), then run the command below. The Kotlin twin needs kotlinc running on JDK 24 or later.
Compare the constant-pool counts with the javap -v listing you read in lesson 2.
describe builds a string and calls nothing else, yet its count is 0. Before reading on: which instruction does it contain, and why didn't the filter count it?

code.title: ClassFileTour.java (JDK 24+)
code.html: // JDK 24 or later (the ClassFile API is final since JDK 24, JEP 484). From labs/: // java bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.java [path/to/Some.class] // With no argument it reads StackDemo.class from lesson 2 (run that demo once first), // or java.lang.Integer from the running JDK if the file isn't there. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile; import java.lang.classfile.ClassModel; import java.lang.classfile.MethodModel; import java.lang.classfile.constantpool.PoolEntry; import java.lang.classfile.instruction.InvokeInstruction; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; public class ClassFileTour { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Path p = Path.of(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class"); byte[] bytes = Files.exists(p) ? Files.readAllBytes(p) : Integer.class.getResourceAsStream("Integer.class").readAllBytes(); // 1. parse: an immutable model, inflated lazily as you ask for parts ClassModel cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes); System.out.println(cm.thisClass().asInternalName() + " extends " + cm.superclass().map(c -> c.asInternalName()).orElse("-") + ", major " + cm.majorVersion()); // 2. the constant pool, counted by kind of entry Map<String, Integer> kinds = new TreeMap<>(); for (PoolEntry e : cm.constantPool()) { kinds.merge(e.getClass().getInterfaces()[0].getSimpleName(), 1, Integer::sum); } System.out.println("constant pool: " + kinds); // 3. methods, and the invoke instructions inside each one for (MethodModel m : cm.methods()) { long invokes = m.code() .map(code -> code.elementStream().filter(e -> e instanceof InvokeInstruction).count()) .orElse(0L); System.out.println(" " + m.methodName().stringValue() + m.methodType().stringValue() + " invokes=" + invokes); } } }

alt.title: ClassFileTour.kt (JDK 24+)
alt.html: // JDK 24 or later, with kotlinc running on that JDK. From labs/: // kotlinc bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.kt -jvm-target 21 -include-runtime -d build/cftour.jar // java -jar build/cftour.jar [path/to/Some.class] // With no argument it reads StackDemo.class from lesson 2, or java.lang.Integer from the JDK. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile import java.lang.classfile.instruction.InvokeInstruction import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.Path fun main(args: Array<String>) { val p = Path.of(args.firstOrNull() ?: "bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class") val bytes = if (Files.exists(p)) Files.readAllBytes(p) else Int::class.javaObjectType.getResourceAsStream("Integer.class")!!.readAllBytes() // 1. parse: an immutable model, inflated lazily as you ask for parts val cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes) println("${cm.thisClass().asInternalName()} extends ${cm.superclass().map { it.asInternalName() }.orElse("-")}, major ${cm.majorVersion()}") // 2. the constant pool, counted by kind of entry val kinds = cm.constantPool().groupingBy { it.javaClass.interfaces[0].simpleName }.eachCount().toSortedMap() println("constant pool: $kinds") // 3. methods, and the invoke instructions inside each one for (m in cm.methods()) { val invokes = m.code().map { code -> code.elementStream().filter { it is InvokeInstruction }.count() }.orElse(0L) println(" ${m.methodName().stringValue()}${m.methodType().stringValue()} invokes=$invokes") } }

try.expect: workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo extends java/lang/Object, major 65, a pool with Utf8Entry=43, LongEntry=2 (1000 and 32) and one InvokeDynamicEntry, then four methods: <init>()V invokes=1, seconds(JI)J invokes=0, describe(...) invokes=0 and main(...) invokes=3. describe contains an invokedynamic, lesson 3's string concatenation, which the API models as InvokeDynamicInstruction, a separate type from InvokeInstruction.

sections.h: Printing a new class: builders, and a proofreader called verify
sections.html:
To print a class, you don't create builder objects yourself. You pass lambdas, and the library hands each one the builder for its level: a ClassBuilder for the class, a CodeBuilder for a method body. A CodeBuilder has one method per instruction, so a method body reads like the javap listings of lesson 2. Here is lesson 2's fade again, as a class of its own. Fade.seconds(steps) says how long a fade of that many 32-millisecond steps runs, in whole seconds:

Java
byte[] fade = ClassFile.of().build(ClassDesc.of("Fade"), clb -> clb
        .withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_FINAL)
        .withMethodBody("seconds", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC,
                cob -> cob
                        .lload(0)          // the number of steps, slots 0 and 1
                        .ldc(32L)          // one step, in milliseconds
                        .lmul()
                        .ldc(1_000L)
                        .ldiv()
                        .lreturn()));
Class<?> c = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(fade);   // load it next to this class
Kotlin
val fade = ClassFile.of().build(ClassDesc.of("Fade")) { clb ->
    clb.withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_FINAL)
    clb.withMethodBody("seconds", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_STATIC) { cob ->
        cob.lload(0)                       // the number of steps, slots 0 and 1
            .loadConstant(32L)             // one step, in milliseconds (Kotlin: see below)
            .lmul()
            .loadConstant(1_000L)
            .ldiv()
            .lreturn()
    }
}
val c = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(fade)               // load it next to this class

Read it the way lesson 2's stagehand would. lload(0) puts the number of steps on the pile of cue cards; a long takes local slots 0 and 1. ldc(32L) pushes the step length, and lmul multiplies the top two cards. ldc(1_000L) and ldiv turn milliseconds into seconds, and lreturn hands back the long on top. Then MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass loads the bytes as a class, in the same package and class loader as the class that calls it. (The demo's Fade also gets an empty debugTrace method, for the next section.) The demo prints:

built Fade: 198 bytes, verify errors []
Fade.seconds(12500) = 400

That's 400 seconds, the same fade that lesson 2's StackDemo printed.

The builder writes what you tell it to, including nonsense. A method declared to return an int that pushes a String builds without a complaint. Lesson 1 showed what happens when such a class loads: defineClass can succeed, and a VerifyError arrives later. ClassFile.of().verify(bytes) runs the verifier's checks on the bytes first and returns a list of errors. The verifier is the JVM's proofreader. It checks that every instruction finds values of the right type, and it never reads the plot:

verify(Broken): [java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack in Broken::answer() @2 (integer_type is not assignable from java/lang/String)]

An empty list proves less than it seems. Delete the ldiv, and the class still verifies. Two long values are left on the stack at lreturn, which is legal, and seconds(12500) returns 1000, the last value pushed. You'll try it in a moment.

verify proves that generated code is type-safe, not that it's right. Test what it computes.

Kotlin has one trap here. ldc takes a java.lang.constant.ConstantDesc, an interface that Java's String and Long implement. Kotlin's String and Long types don't show that interface, so cob.ldc("forty-two") doesn't compile in Kotlin. Use loadConstant(32L), which has overloads for primitives, or pass a glossary entry: cob.ldc(cob.constantPool().stringEntry("forty-two")).

We can print new pages now. The harder job is to edit a page that already exists without smudging the rest.

try.title: Build, verify, then break it
steps: On JDK 24 or later, run ClassFileForge from labs/ (command below), or build and run the Kotlin twin.
Read the first three lines: the size of the generated class, its verify result, the fade length, and the verifier's message for Broken.
In the seconds body, delete the .ldiv() line, and predict what verify(fade) reports and what seconds(12500) returns. Run it again.

code.title: ClassFileForge.java (JDK 24+)
code.html: // JDK 24 or later (the ClassFile API is final since JDK 24, JEP 484). From labs/: // java bytecode/preview/ClassFileForge.java // Builds a class from scratch, verifies a broken one, then transforms the first. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile; import java.lang.classfile.ClassModel; import java.lang.classfile.ClassTransform; import java.lang.classfile.CodeTransform; import java.lang.classfile.MethodModel; import java.lang.classfile.instruction.ConstantInstruction; import java.lang.constant.ClassDesc; import java.lang.constant.MethodTypeDesc; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_String; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_int; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_long; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_void; public class ClassFileForge { public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable { ClassFile cf = ClassFile.of(); // 1. build: a class with seconds(long steps) = steps * 32 / 1_000 and a debug method byte[] fade = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("Fade"), clb -> clb .withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_FINAL) .withMethodBody("seconds", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob .lload(0) // push the number of steps (slots 0 and 1) .ldc(32L) // push the length of one step, in milliseconds .lmul() .ldc(1_000L) .ldiv() .lreturn()) .withMethodBody("debugTrace", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_void, CD_String), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob .return_())); System.out.println("built Fade: " + fade.length + " bytes, verify errors " + cf.verify(fade)); Class<?> c1 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(fade); System.out.println("Fade.seconds(12500) = " + c1.getMethod("seconds", long.class).invoke(null, 12_500L)); // 2. verify before you load: an int method that returns a String byte[] broken = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("Broken"), clb -> clb .withMethodBody("answer", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_int), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob.ldc("forty-two").ireturn())); System.out.println("verify(Broken): " + cf.verify(broken)); // 3. transform: drop debug methods and change the 32 constant to 40, as a new class FadeV2 ClassModel model = cf.parse(fade); CodeTransform slower = (cob, element) -> { if (element instanceof ConstantInstruction ci && Long.valueOf(32L).equals(ci.constantValue())) { cob.ldc(40L); // replace this element } else { cob.with(element); // pass everything else through unchanged } }; ClassTransform transform = ClassTransform .dropping(e -> e instanceof MethodModel m && m.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug")) .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(slower)); byte[] v2 = cf.transformClass(model, ClassDesc.of("FadeV2"), transform); Class<?> c2 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(v2); System.out.println("FadeV2 methods " + cf.parse(v2).methods().stream().map(m -> m.methodName().stringValue()).toList() + ", seconds(12500) = " + c2.getMethod("seconds", long.class).invoke(null, 12_500L)); } }

ClassFile.of() val static = ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_STATIC // 1. build: a class with seconds(long steps) = steps * 32 / 1_000 and a debug method val fade = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("Fade")) { clb -> clb.withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_FINAL) clb.withMethodBody("seconds", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), static) { cob -> cob.lload(0) // push the number of steps (slots 0 and 1) .loadConstant(32L) // push the length of one step, in milliseconds (ldc2_w) .lmul() .loadConstant(1_000L) .ldiv() .lreturn() } clb.withMethodBody("debugTrace", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_void, CD_String), static) { cob -> cob.return_() } } println("built Fade: ${fade.size} bytes, verify errors ${cf.verify(fade)}") val c1 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(fade) println("Fade.seconds(12500) = ${c1.getMethod("seconds", Long::class.javaPrimitiveType).invoke(null, 12_500L)}") // 2. verify before you load: an int method that returns a String val broken = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("Broken")) { clb -> clb.withMethodBody("answer", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_int), static) { cob -> // Kotlin's String type doesn't expose Java's ConstantDesc, so pass a constant-pool entry cob.ldc(cob.constantPool().stringEntry("forty-two")).ireturn() } } println("verify(Broken): ${cf.verify(broken)}") // 3. transform: drop debug methods and change the 32 constant to 40, as a new class FadeV2 val slower = CodeTransform { cob, element -> if (element is ConstantInstruction && element.constantValue().equals(32L)) { cob.loadConstant(40L) // replace this element } else { cob.with(element) // pass everything else through unchanged } } val transform = ClassTransform .dropping { it is MethodModel && it.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug") } .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(slower)) val v2 = cf.transformClass(cf.parse(fade), ClassDesc.of("FadeV2"), transform) val c2 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(v2) println("FadeV2 methods ${cf.parse(v2).methods().map { it.methodName().stringValue() }}, " + "seconds(12500) = ${c2.getMethod("seconds", Long::class.javaPrimitiveType).invoke(null, 12_500L)}") }

try.expect: built Fade: 198 bytes, verify errors [], Fade.seconds(12500) = 400, and verify(Broken): [java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack in Broken::answer() @2 (integer_type is not assignable from java/lang/String)]. Without ldiv, the class is 197 bytes and still verifies with no errors, and seconds(12500) returns 1000. Two longs are left on the stack at lreturn, which the verifier allows, and the method returns the one on top, the last value pushed. The verifier proves the code is type-safe, not that it's right.

sections.h: Editing a class safely: a transform keeps, drops or replaces each element
sections.html:
Changing an existing class is where elements pay off. The package documentation puts it in one sentence: "Transformation can be viewed as a 'flatMap' operation on the sequence of elements; for every element, we could pass it through unchanged, drop it, or replace it with one or more elements." (flatMap is the stream operation that turns each item into zero, one or more items.)

Picture copying a page of the prompt book line by line. For each line you can copy it as it is, leave it out, or write something else in its place. A ClassTransform sees a class's elements, and a CodeTransform sees the instructions of one method. Inside a transform, you hand each element to the builder: builder.with(element) passes it through, doing nothing drops it, and calling other builder methods replaces it. This transform drops every method whose name starts with debug, and makes every fade slower, with 40 ms steps instead of 32:

Java
CodeTransform slower = (cob, element) -> {
    if (element instanceof ConstantInstruction ci && Long.valueOf(32L).equals(ci.constantValue())) {
        cob.ldc(40L);             // replace
    } else {
        cob.with(element);        // pass through
    }
};
ClassTransform transform = ClassTransform
        .dropping(e -> e instanceof MethodModel m && m.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug"))
        .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(slower));
byte[] v2 = cf.transformClass(cf.parse(fade), ClassDesc.of("FadeV2"), transform);
Kotlin
val slower = CodeTransform { cob, element ->
    if (element is ConstantInstruction && element.constantValue().equals(32L)) {
        cob.loadConstant(40L)     // replace
    } else {
        cob.with(element)         // pass through
    }
}
val transform = ClassTransform
    .dropping { it is MethodModel && it.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug") }
    .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(slower))
val v2 = cf.transformClass(cf.parse(fade), ClassDesc.of("FadeV2"), transform)

The new class, FadeV2, has only seconds left, and the same 12,500 steps now take longer:

FadeV2 methods [seconds], seconds(12500) = 500

Everything the transform passed through was copied unchanged. That's also the default: a transform that changes nothing reproduces the class.

The JDK prints its own classes on this press. ProxyGenerator moved from its internal ASM to java.lang.classfile in JDK 23, and the lambda class generator, InnerClassLambdaMetafactory, followed in JDK 24. So on JDK 25, the $Proxy0 of lesson 4 and the $$Lambda classes of lesson 3 come from the code you just ran.

Who should use it? A tool that only needs to run on JDK 24 or later can drop its ASM dependency, because the API always matches the JDK it runs on. A library that must support older JDKs can't. Byte Buddy's regular jar targets Java 8 and its -jdk5 jar targets Java 5, so it keeps its bundled ASM and bridges to the ClassFile API when it finds one. Its release notes for 1.16.0 say: "Include support for JDK Class File API".

To edit a class, copy it element by element. Pass through everything you don't mean to change.

Here's the limit of today's tool. Every class in this lesson was new: we printed Fade, then copied it into FadeV2 under a new name. A class that is already loaded, with objects already using it, can't be replaced by defining another class. Changing that one takes an agent.

try.title: Write your own transform
steps: Run ClassFileForge again and read the last line.
Change the code transform so it also turns 1_000L into 60_000L, so that the method returns minutes, without touching the 32 branch. Predict the new FadeV2.seconds(12500) before you run it.
Undo that, then remove the .andThen(...) part, keeping only dropping. Which number in the last line changes?

code.title: ClassFileForge.java (JDK 24+)
code.html: // JDK 24 or later (the ClassFile API is final since JDK 24, JEP 484). From labs/: // java bytecode/preview/ClassFileForge.java // Builds a class from scratch, verifies a broken one, then transforms the first. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile; import java.lang.classfile.ClassModel; import java.lang.classfile.ClassTransform; import java.lang.classfile.CodeTransform; import java.lang.classfile.MethodModel; import java.lang.classfile.instruction.ConstantInstruction; import java.lang.constant.ClassDesc; import java.lang.constant.MethodTypeDesc; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_String; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_int; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_long; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_void; public class ClassFileForge { public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable { ClassFile cf = ClassFile.of(); // 1. build: a class with seconds(long steps) = steps * 32 / 1_000 and a debug method byte[] fade = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("Fade"), clb -> clb .withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_FINAL) .withMethodBody("seconds", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob .lload(0) // push the number of steps (slots 0 and 1) .ldc(32L) // push the length of one step, in milliseconds .lmul() .ldc(1_000L) .ldiv() .lreturn()) .withMethodBody("debugTrace", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_void, CD_String), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob .return_())); System.out.println("built Fade: " + fade.length + " bytes, verify errors " + cf.verify(fade)); Class<?> c1 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(fade); System.out.println("Fade.seconds(12500) = " + c1.getMethod("seconds", long.class).invoke(null, 12_500L)); // 2. verify before you load: an int method that returns a String byte[] broken = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("Broken"), clb -> clb .withMethodBody("answer", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_int), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob.ldc("forty-two").ireturn())); System.out.println("verify(Broken): " + cf.verify(broken)); // 3. transform: drop debug methods and change the 32 constant to 40, as a new class FadeV2 ClassModel model = cf.parse(fade); CodeTransform slower = (cob, element) -> { if (element instanceof ConstantInstruction ci && Long.valueOf(32L).equals(ci.constantValue())) { cob.ldc(40L); // replace this element } else { cob.with(element); // pass everything else through unchanged } }; ClassTransform transform = ClassTransform .dropping(e -> e instanceof MethodModel m && m.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug")) .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(slower)); byte[] v2 = cf.transformClass(model, ClassDesc.of("FadeV2"), transform); Class<?> c2 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(v2); System.out.println("FadeV2 methods " + cf.parse(v2).methods().stream().map(m -> m.methodName().stringValue()).toList() + ", seconds(12500) = " + c2.getMethod("seconds", long.class).invoke(null, 12_500L)); } }

try.expect: Before your change: FadeV2 methods [seconds], seconds(12500) = 500. With both constants replaced: 12,500 x 40 / 60,000 = 8. The fade lasts 8 minutes and 20 seconds, and integer division quietly drops the 20. With only dropping, FadeV2 still loses debugTrace, but seconds keeps the 32 and returns 400 again.

compare.title: Reading a class's name in Java and Kotlin, by hand and with the API

java.title: ThisClass.java
java.html: // by hand (any JDK): walk the pool, then read this_class static String thisClass(byte[] bytes) { return ClassFileFacts.thisClass(bytes); // the lab's DataInputStream walk } // with the ClassFile API (JDK 24+) static String thisClassWithApi(byte[] bytes) { return ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).thisClass().asInternalName(); }

kotlin.title: ThisClass.kt
kotlin.html: // by hand (any JDK): walk the pool, then read this_class fun thisClass(bytes: ByteArray): String = ClassFileFacts.thisClass(bytes) // the lab's DataInputStream walk // with the ClassFile API (JDK 24+) fun thisClassWithApi(bytes: ByteArray): String = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).thisClass().asInternalName()

compare.note: Same bytes, same answer. The API version is one line, because the library walks the pool for you, and only as far as it needs to. The language differences are small but real. Kotlin calls the API through ordinary SAM conversion for its Consumer and CodeTransform parameters, and writes access flags with or instead of |. Kotlin's String and Long types don't show Java's ConstantDesc, so ldc("...") needs a constant-pool entry, or loadConstant for primitives. And compiling Kotlin against the API needs kotlinc to run on JDK 24 or later (or to point -jdk-home at one), whatever -jvm-target you choose.

worked.title: Find the jar that broke the start-up

steps.say: The theatre's ticket app starts on JDK 21 and stops at once. A jar is a zip file of class files, and the app is built from several of them. Which part of the message tells you what to look for?
steps.code:
Error: LinkageError occurred while loading main class theatre.booking.SeatMap
	java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: theatre/booking/SeatMap has been compiled by a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 65.0

steps.say: Class file version 69.0 is Java 25 (69 - 44), and the runtime only knows up to 65, Java 21. Something was compiled for JDK 25. Here one class is named, but a jar can mix versions, so check every class. Read each entry's header with the lab's code.
steps.code: try (JarFile jar = new JarFile(path.toFile())) { jar.stream() .filter(e -> e.getName().endsWith(".class")) .forEach(e -> { try (InputStream in = jar.getInputStream(e)) { // 1. read magic, minor, major from the first 10 bytes ClassFileFacts.Header h = ClassFileFacts.header(in.readNBytes(10)); // 2. report anything newer than the runtime if (h.major() > 65) System.out.println(e.getName() + " -> Java " + ClassFileFacts.javaVersion(h.major())); } catch (IOException ex) { throw new UncheckedIOException(ex); } }); }

alt.html: JarFile(path.toFile()).use { jar -> jar.stream() .filter { it.name.endsWith(".class") } .forEach { e -> // 1. read magic, minor, major from the first 10 bytes val h = jar.getInputStream(e).use { ClassFileFacts.header(it.readNBytes(10)) } // 2. report anything newer than the runtime if (h.major() > 65) println("${e.name} -> Java ${ClassFileFacts.javaVersion(h.major())}") } }

steps.say: Two caveats. A multi-release jar, one that carries extra copies of classes for newer JDKs, keeps them under META-INF/versions/25/, and those are allowed: the JVM only loads them on JDK 25. So skip that prefix, or you'll get false alarms. And module-info.class has a version too. When the culprit is your own code, the fix is in the build: compile with --release 21 (in Gradle, options.release.set(21)) and jvmTarget = 21 for Kotlin, as the labs do, so the compilers also refuse APIs newer than JDK 21.

lab.title: Read the constant pool by hand
steps: Run the tests once. All seven fail. Read the class-file layout and the tag table in the Javadoc of ClassFileFacts.

Write header: wrap the bytes in a DataInputStream, read the int magic and throw IllegalArgumentException (with "magic" in the message) if it isn't 0xCAFEBABE, then read three unsigned shorts. Write javaVersion as major - 44, rejecting anything below 49.

Write a private pool walk: for i from 1 to count - 1, read the tag, then either keep the value (readUTF() for tag 1, the name index for tag 7) or skip the right number of bytes. After a tag 5 or 6, add one more to i.
Write referencedClasses with the walk: the Utf8 string at each Class entry's name index. Write thisClass: after the walk, read access_flags, then this_class, and look up its name.
Run the tests until all seven pass. The expected answers come from ASM, so a pass means your reader agrees with a production library on Java, Kotlin and JDK classes.
hints: A wrong byte count anywhere in the walk shifts everything after it, so the symptom is usually unknown constant pool tag far from the bug. Check the table entry for the last tag you handled.
DataInputStream.readUTF() reads a two-byte length and then the bytes, in the class file's own "modified UTF-8". That's exactly a Utf8 entry, so you don't decode anything yourself.
Forgetting the extra index after Long and Double passes for some classes and fails for Fixture, which has both.

drill.title: The constant pool walk from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page and the lab. Write the loop that walks a constant pool with a DataInputStream, given count. Handle Utf8, Class, the fixed-size entries and the two-index entries. Then check: which tags take two pool indexes, and which entry has a 3-byte body?

answer.html: for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) { // index 0 is never used int tag = in.readUnsignedByte(); switch (tag) { case 1 -> utf8[i] = in.readUTF(); // Utf8: u2 length + bytes case 7 -> classNameIndex[i] = in.readUnsignedShort(); case 8, 16, 19, 20 -> in.skipBytes(2); // String, MethodType, Module, Package case 15 -> in.skipBytes(3); // MethodHandle: u1 kind + u2 index case 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 12, 17, 18 -> in.skipBytes(4); case 5, 6 -> { in.skipBytes(8); i++; } // Long, Double: two indexes default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("tag " + tag + " at " + i); } }

alt.html: var i = 1 // index 0 is never used while (i < count) { when (val tag = input.readUnsignedByte()) { 1 -> utf8[i] = input.readUTF() // Utf8: u2 length + bytes 7 -> classNameIndex[i] = input.readUnsignedShort() 8, 16, 19, 20 -> input.skipBytes(2) // String, MethodType, Module, Package 15 -> input.skipBytes(3) // MethodHandle: u1 kind + u2 index 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 12, 17, 18 -> input.skipBytes(4) 5, 6 -> { input.skipBytes(8); i++ } // Long, Double: two indexes else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("tag $tag at $i") } i++ }

recap: A class file starts with CAFEBABE, the minor and major version (Java version = major - 44 from Java 5 on: 65 is 21, 69 is 25), then the constant pool.
Each pool entry starts with a tag that fixes its size; Long and Double take two indexes. this_class comes right after the pool and the access flags.

The ClassFile API (java.lang.classfile) was a preview in JDK 22 and 23 and became final in JDK 24 (JEP 484). Labs built with release 21 can't use it, so its code runs as single-file programs on JDK 24 or later.
ClassFile.of().parse gives a lazy, immutable ClassModel, which is also a sequence of elements, such as methods or instructions. build takes builder lambdas.
verify checks type safety before loading, not correctness, and transformClass copies a class element by element: pass with with, drop by doing nothing, or replace.
The limit: these tools make new classes. Changing a class that is already loaded, under objects that use it, needs an agent.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why a hand-written constant-pool walk is fiddly, what the ClassFile API's model, builder and transform each give you, and why the API's arrival in JDK 24 matters for tools that write classes.
explain.answer: A class file stores every name and constant in a numbered pool, and each entry's size depends on its tag. You must handle every tag, and Long and Double take two indexes, so one wrong count misreads everything after it. The ClassFile API does that walk for you. parse gives an immutable, lazily parsed model of the class, its methods and their code, which you can read as sequences of typed elements. build takes lambdas that receive builders with one method per instruction, and verify checks type safety before you load the result, though not whether it computes the right thing. transformClass copies a class while you decide, element by element, to pass it through, drop it or replace it. Before JDK 24 the JDK had no public library, so tools bundled ASM and needed a new release for each class-file version. The API always matches the JDK it runs on, and the JDK now builds its own proxies and lambdas with it.

deeper.html:
Three details from the API's documentation and this track's runs.

Models are lazy, and that can surprise you. parse reads little more than the header. A method's code is inflated when you ask for it, so a broken method can parse fine and fail with IllegalArgumentException later, when you iterate its elements. If you run untrusted or generated bytes through the API, iterate or verify them up front.

The ClassFile API and Byte Buddy work at different levels. Byte Buddy works with types and methods (extend this class, intercept those methods with that delegate), and it runs on JDK 8. The ClassFile API works with the class file itself (these instructions, that constant), and it needs JDK 24. Byte Buddy's README says that "as of 1.17.0, support will extend to new Java versions unless previously unknown class file features are discovered. This is possible through Byte Buddy's support of the Class File API." So on a new JDK, Byte Buddy can lean on the JDK's own reader and writer.

ConstantPool is an Iterable<PoolEntry>, not a collection, so Java needs StreamSupport to stream it, while Kotlin's Iterable extensions work on it directly:

Java
// JDK 24+: every Class entry a class references, with the API
Set<String> names = StreamSupport.stream(ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).constantPool().spliterator(), false)
        .filter(e -> e instanceof ClassEntry)
        .map(e -> ((ClassEntry) e).asInternalName())
        .collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));
Kotlin
// JDK 24+: every Class entry a class references, with the API
val names = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).constantPool()
    .filterIsInstance<ClassEntry>()
    .map { it.asInternalName() }
    .toSortedSet()

sources.title: JVM Specification SE 25, chapter 4: The class File Format
